analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rates for individuals roughly in half, from 10% and 20% to 5% and 10%.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee: after its April 2001 introduction it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the two main federal tax rates on profits from selling stocks, property, and other investments, from 10% and 20% down to 5% and 10%. It would also apply those lower rates under the alternative minimum tax and repeal a temporary provision that had given an extra break to people who held assets for at least five years. Because capital gains are realized overwhelmingly by higher-income households that own most of the stocks and other taxable assets, the tax savings would flow mainly to those households, while the federal government would collect less revenue that otherwise supports spending or deficit reduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell appreciated assets — primarily higher-income households, since asset ownership and realized capital gains are concentrated at the top of the income distribution. A household whose main income is wages and salary would generally owe no capital gains tax and so would get little or nothing from the rate cut. Financial firms that manage, trade, and broker those assets would also benefit indirectly, since lower rates make holding and selling investments more attractive.

how_it_helps.text: The bill cuts the two main individual capital gains rates from 10% and 20% to 5% and 10%, halving the tax owed on profits from selling stocks, real estate, and other assets held more than the required holding period.
It applies the same lower 5% and 10% rates under the alternative minimum tax, so investors who owe AMT would also pay the reduced rates on their capital gains.
It repeals the temporary reduced rates for qualified five-year gains, replacing that complicated holding-period structure with the single lower rate schedule.
The new rates would apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 2000, so the cut would be retroactive to the current tax year.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect less revenue from the tax on investment profits. If the cut were not paired with spending cuts, ordinary taxpayers would eventually bear it through a larger national debt, through other taxes, or through reduced government services.

drawbacks.text: The benefits would be highly concentrated: capital gains are realized mainly by higher-income households that own most stocks and taxable assets, so a rate cut delivers most of its savings to them while reducing revenue available for everything else the government does.
Cutting the top rate from 20% to 10% is a large revenue loss for the Treasury, which either widens the deficit or forces offsetting tax increases or spending cuts elsewhere.

Supporters' best argument — that lower rates reward saving and encourage investment and economic growth — rests on the claim that cheaper taxes on gains increase capital formation; the counterargument is that the same money could fund services or debt reduction with more immediate benefit to people whose income comes from work, not assets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits go almost entirely to households that own taxable investments, which skews strongly toward the top of the income distribution, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across everyone or pushed onto the national debt. For a household living on wages, the bill offers essentially nothing and costs something. The case for it rests on the secondary claim that cheaper taxes on investment encourage growth that eventually helps everyone; even granting that argument, the immediate and certain beneficiaries are asset owners.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Collins introduced the Capital Gains Tax Rate Reduction Act of 2001 on April 3, 2001, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
Twenty-one members cosponsored the bill — 20 Republicans and 1 Independent.
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action; there is no record of a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the Treasury kept collecting capital gains revenue at the existing rates, and no broad new tax cut flowing mainly to high-income asset owners took effect through this bill. Asset owners did not get the savings it offered, and everyone else was spared the revenue loss it would have caused.

for.name: Rep. Mac Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 3, 2001 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 20 of 223 House Republicans and 1 of 1 House Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small, nearly all-Republican base of support.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on April 3, 2001 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so the partisan shape can only be inferred from sponsorship: 20 of the 21 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill died in a committee then controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: These households would have been the bill's main beneficiaries, roughly halving the tax on profits from selling stocks, businesses, and property. Because the bill died, they did not get this cut. Their interest in the bill ran against the general public's stake in federal revenue.

Brokers, mutual funds, and asset managers would have benefited indirectly: a much lower tax on gains makes buying and selling assets more attractive, which supports the industry's fees and trading volume. The bill's death left that incentive unchanged.
